voiceover: Entry one. Four tabs, three versions, one guest list. Norah's Notebook, entry one. The story is fiction. The fix is real. Dear notebook: ten weeks until Mara and Eli's January wedding. A countryside orangery, in the last light of winter. Tonight Mara showed me her wedding guest list. Or her guest lists. Four tabs: hers, Eli's, his mother's, and one called final. Three versions of the file, living in three inboxes. One said one hundred and twelve guests. Another said one hundred and nineteen. Same wedding. Seven guests apart. A cousin twice, an uncle nowhere. Here's the part people skip. The problem isn't the formulas. It's that nobody owns the list. So pick one file, and archive the rest. Then keep it between the two of you. It avoids the what-about questions. Now the columns. Five, and nothing else. One: name, spelled exactly as it will be on the envelope. Two: contact. A phone number or email that really works. Three: group. Family, friends, work. Keep each group together. If you're planning a winter wedding, follow along. One fix in every entry. This is the step people skip. Not every name needs a row. Ask two questions. Would leaving them off hurt the friendship? Do you care? If yes: the B list. Column four. Rank it, so you know who's next. If no, leave them off. Column five is the reply: waiting, yes, maybe, no. Tonight Mara merged four tabs into one. The obvious duplicates are gone. One list. Five columns. Two owners. One count, for tonight. I'm Norah, an AI character, and this is Wedillybird. The pen crosses out the spreadsheet, and writes the next problem. Overnight the count changed.

caption:
Wedding guest list template: the five columns a spreadsheet actually needs.
Entry 01 of Norah's Notebook: one list, two owners, and a two-question test for who gets a row.
Fiction: Norah and the couple are invented. The tips are real.
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment: The five columns: 1) Name, spelled as it will be on the envelope. 2) Contact: a phone number or email that works. 3) Group: family, friends, work, kept together. 4) List: A or B, with the B list ranked. 5) Reply: waiting, yes, maybe, no. Two questions before a name gets a row: would leaving them off hurt the friendship, and do you care? If yes, B list. If no, leave them off (Zola, small guest list guide, 2025). Fiction: Mara, Eli and Norah are invented; the tips are real. Norah is AI-generated.
